content: The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine is used to provide immunity or protection against tuberculosis (TB). It is typically administered to individuals who are at high risk of developing TB. Additionally, the BCG vaccine is used as a treatment for bladder tumors or bladder cancer. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other purposes. If you have questions about its use, consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. This medication is administered by a healthcare provider. When used for TB prevention, it is injected into the skin. After receiving the vaccine, you should keep the injection site dry for 24 hours and maintain cleanliness until the area is indistinguishable from the surrounding skin. When used for bladder cancer treatment, the medication is introduced into the bladder through a catheter. You should avoid drinking fluids for four hours before the treatment and empty your bladder beforehand. During the first hour after the medication is infused, you will need to lie on your stomach, back, and sides for 15 minutes each. Afterward, you will stand but must retain the medication in your bladder for an additional hour. If you are unable to hold the medication for the full two hours, inform your healthcare provider. At the end of the two-hour period, you will empty your bladder while seated for safety reasons. Your urine must be disinfected for six hours after the medication is administered. To do this, pour an equal amount of undiluted bleach into the toilet after urinating, let it sit for 15 minutes, and then flush. The dosing schedule may vary, and your doctor will determine the appropriate treatment plan. If you do not understand any instructions, ask your doctor for clarification. For TB prevention, the vaccine is usually given only once but may be repeated if there is no adequate response within 2–3 months. The response is assessed using a TB skin test. Before receiving the BCG vaccine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to the BCG vaccine or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially antibiotics, cancer chemotherapy agents, steroids, tuberculosis medications, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have recently received a smallpox vaccination or if you have had a positive TB test. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have an immune disorder, cancer, fever, infection, or severe burns on your body. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, let your doctor know. If you become pregnant while receiving the BCG vaccine, contact your doctor immediately. The BCG vaccine may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: swollen lymph nodes, small red areas at the injection site (these typically appear 10–14 days after injection, gradually decrease in size, and should disappear within about six months), fever, blood in the urine, frequent or painful urination, upset stomach, or vomiting. If you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately: severe skin rash, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or wheezing. In the event of an overdose, call your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Ensure that you keep all appointments with your doctor and the laboratory for follow-up care and monitoring.
